tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

**Title:** ParallelSpec: Parallel Drafter for Efficient Speculative Decoding

**Authors:** Zilin Xiao, Hongming Zhang, Tao Ge, Siru Ouyang, Vicente Ordonez, Dong Yu

**First version (v1) submitted:** Tue, 8 Oct 2024, 01:05:08 UTC (2,858 KB)

**All versions:** Only v1 is listed (8 Oct 2024).

**Comments field:** "work in progress". No venue is given.

**Journal-ref:** None is listed on the page.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit, so here is a close summary:

Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference. A small drafter cheaply guesses upcoming tokens, and the target model checks them in parallel. The authors argue that most existing methods still draft tokens one at a time to preserve sequential dependency, which they see as "a huge computational burden in speculative decoding."

They propose ParallelSpec as a replacement for autoregressive drafting. It trains a single parallel drafter that predicts several future tokens at once. It can be plugged into any speculative decoding framework that aligns drafter and target output distributions, "with minimal training cost."

In experiments, it cuts baseline latency by up to 62% on text generation benchmarks across domains. It reaches "2.84X overall speedup on the Llama-2-13B model using third-party evaluation criteria."

The complete abstract is on the arXiv page (arXiv:2410.05589).

**Title:** AMUSD: Asynchronous Multi-Device Speculative Decoding for LLM Acceleration

**Author:** Bradley McDanel (sole author)

**First version (v1) submitted:** Tuesday, 22 October 2024, 19:15:35 UTC (226 KB)

**All versions:** Only v1 is listed (22 Oct 2024).

**Comments field:** "4 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, 1 algorithm". It gives no venue information.

**Journal-ref:** None is listed on the page.

**Abstract (paraphrased, since I can't reproduce the full text verbatim):**
LLMs normally produce text one token at a time, with each output feeding the next step. Speculative decoding speeds this up by having a small, fast draft model propose candidate tokens, which the larger original model then checks in parallel. This paper presents AMUSD, which separates drafting and verification into a continuous, asynchronous process. In standard speculative decoding, only one model generates at any given moment. AMUSD instead lets both models run predictions independently on separate devices such as GPUs. Across several datasets, the author reports "an average 29% improvement over speculative decoding and up to 1.96× speedup over conventional autoregressive decoding," with output quality unchanged. The code is open source on GitHub (github.com/BradMcDanel/AMUSD).

**Subjects:** cs.CL (primary), cs.DC, cs.LG. **DOI:** 10.48550/arXiv.2410.17375. **License:** CC BY 4.0.

**Title:** "SuffixDecoding: Extreme Speculative Decoding for Emerging AI Applications" (arXiv:2411.04975)

**Authors:** Gabriele Oliaro, Zhihao Jia, Daniel Campos, Aurick Qiao. The page's PDF link text says "Gabriele Oliaro and 2 other authors," which conflicts with the four names listed.

**First version (v1):** Thursday, 7 Nov 2024, 18:49:33 UTC

**All versions:**
- v1: 7 Nov 2024 (318 KB)
- v2: 2 Jun 2025 (1,139 KB)
- v3: 7 Oct 2025 (1,134 KB), the current version

**Comments field:** "NeurIPS 2025 (Spotlight)"

**Journal-ref:** None is listed on the page.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit. Here is a summary:
- Speculative decoding usually relies on smaller draft models to cut LLM inference latency.
- Agentic workloads differ from ordinary use. Multi-agent pipelines and self-refinement loops send repetitive requests that yield "long and highly predictable sequences," and existing methods don't exploit them well.
- SuffixDecoding uses suffix trees to cache long token sequences from prompts and earlier outputs.
- It adapts how many tokens it speculates: more when acceptance is likely, fewer when it isn't, which saves compute.
- On agentic benchmarks such as SWE-Bench and Text-to-SQL, it achieves "speedups of up to 5.3×."
- It is 2.8× faster than model-based methods like EAGLE-2/3 and 1.9× faster than model-free Token Recycling.
- The code is open-sourced at github.com/snowflakedb/ArcticInference.

The full text is available at arxiv.org/abs/2411.04975 under a CC BY 4.0 license.

**Title:** "LogitSpec: Accelerating Retrieval-based Speculative Decoding via Next Next Token Speculation" (arXiv:2507.01449, cs.CL)

**Authors:** Tianyu Liu, Qitan Lv, Hao Li, Xing Gao, Xiao Sun, Xiaoyan Sun

**First version (v1):** Wednesday, 2 July 2025, 08:08:30 UTC (238 KB)

**All versions:**
- v1: 2 Jul 2025 (238 KB)
- v2: 12 Jan 2026, 09:32:48 UTC (271 KB)
- v3: 29 Apr 2026, 08:32:18 UTC (272 KB), the current version

**Comments field (venue info):** Not shown on this page.

**Journal-ref:** Not shown on this page.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit, so here is a summary with short quotes:

- **Background:** Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose tokens, which the target model then checks in parallel. Retrieval-based variants remove the draft model to cut overhead and simplify deployment.
- **Problem:** These retrieval methods depend on matching, and they "often fail to find matched and accurate draft tokens."
- **Key observation:** The authors note that the last token's logit "can not only predict the next token, but also speculate the next next token."
- **Method:** LogitSpec drafts in two stages. First, it uses the final logit to guess the token after next. Second, it retrieves references for both the next token and the one after it, which widens the retrieval range.
- **Properties:** The method is "training-free and plug-and-play" and fits into existing LLM inference frameworks.
- **Results:** Across a range of text generation benchmarks, it reaches "up to 2.61× speedup and 3.28 mean accepted tokens per decoding step."
- **Code:** github.com/smart-lty/LogitSpec

The full abstract text is on the arXiv page (license: CC BY 4.0).

**Title:** Traversal Verification for Speculative Tree Decoding (arXiv:2505.12398)

**Authors:** Yepeng Weng, Qiao Hu, Xujie Chen, Li Liu, Dianwen Mei, Huishi Qiu, Jiang Tian, Zhongchao Shi

**First version (v1) submitted:** Sun, 18 May 2025, 12:51:55 UTC

**All versions:**
- v1: 18 May 2025 (265 KB)
- v2: Wed, 5 Nov 2025, 13:59:39 UTC (353 KB), the current version

**Comments:** "NeurIPS 2025 poster"

**Journal-ref:** None is listed on the page.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** I can't reproduce the full abstract word for word because of the quote-length limit, so here is a close summary.

- **Background:** Speculative decoding speeds up large language models. A small draft model guesses several upcoming tokens, and the target model checks them in parallel.
- **Problem:** To raise acceptance, current frameworks build token trees with several candidates per step. They still verify token by token, which causes two problems:
  - A sequence's probability distribution differs from that of single tokens, so acceptance length is suboptimal.
  - Verification runs top-down from the root, layer by layer. When a parent is rejected, all its children are dropped, which wastes candidates.
- **Method:** The paper proposes Traversal Verification, which checks the tree "through leaf-to-root traversal." It evaluates acceptance of the whole sequence from a node back to the root, which keeps subsequences that older methods would discard too early.
- **Theory:** The authors prove the resulting distribution matches the target model's, so inference is lossless.
- **Results:** Experiments across several LLMs and tasks show consistent gains in acceptance length and throughput over existing methods.

content.content:
**Title:** LongSpec: Long-Context Lossless Speculative Decoding with Efficient Drafting and Verification (arXiv:2502.17421, cs.CL; cross-listed cs.AI, cs.LG)

**Authors:** Penghui Yang, Cunxiao Du, Fengzhuo Zhang, Haonan Wang, Tianyu Pang, Chao Du, Bo An

**First version (v1):** Monday, 24 Feb 2025

**Version history:**
- v1: Mon, 24 Feb 2025, 18:53:31 UTC (4,932 KB)
- v2: Tue, 17 Jun 2025, 05:58:01 UTC (5,154 KB)
- v3: Tue, 7 Apr 2026, 07:52:49 UTC (4,919 KB)
- v4: Wed, 8 Apr 2026, 06:06:59 UTC (4,920 KB), the current version

**Comments:** "Accepted by ACL'25 (Main)"

**Journal-ref:** None is listed on the page.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit. Here is a close summary:

- **Motivation:** LLMs can now handle very long inputs, so fast inference over them matters, especially for LLM agents. Speculative decoding (SD) speeds up inference without loss, unlike lossy approaches such as quantization or model cascades.
- **Problem:** Most leading SD methods are trained on short texts, usually under 4k tokens, so they don't suit long contexts. The authors identify three obstacles:
  1. Draft models need a lot of memory because of their large KV cache.
  2. Training on short contexts but running on long ones hurts performance.
  3. Tree attention becomes inefficient over long token sequences.
- **Solution:** LongSpec answers each obstacle in turn:
  1. A draft model whose KV cache stays a fixed size.
  2. New position indices that reduce the train/inference mismatch.
  3. An attention aggregation method that pairs fast prefix computation with standard tree attention.
- **Results:** The paper reports "up to a 3.26x speedup over strong Flash Attention baselines" on five long-context understanding datasets. It also reports a 2.25x cut in wall-clock time on AIME24 long reasoning with the QwQ model.
- **Code:** Released at github.com/sail-sg/LongSpec.

**License:** CC BY 4.0

**Title:** Kangaroo: Lossless Self-Speculative Decoding via Double Early Exiting

**Authors:** Fangcheng Liu, Yehui Tang, Zhenhua Liu, Yunsheng Ni, Kai Han, Yunhe Wang

**First version (v1) submitted:** Monday, 29 April 2024, 17:53:54 UTC (259 KB)

**All versions:** Only v1 is listed (29 April 2024).

**Comments field (venue info):** Not shown on the page.

**Journal-ref:** Not shown on the page.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit, but here is a close summary:

- **Problem:** Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference while keeping the sampling distribution the same. However, training a separate draft model that gets a good token acceptance rate can be expensive.
- **Approach:** Kangaroo is a self-speculative decoding framework inspired by early exiting. It "uses a fixed shallow sub-network as a self-draft model," and the remaining layers act as the larger target model.
- **Adapter:** A lightweight adapter is trained on top of the shallow sub-network. It narrows the representational gap between the sub-network and the full model.
- **Second early exit:** Because the self-draft model's latency may not be negligible, the authors add a second early-exit mechanism during drafting. Drafting stops once the confidence for the current token falls below a threshold. This aims to raise acceptance rates while reducing drafting steps.
- **Results:** On Spec-Bench with single-sequence verification, Kangaroo reaches "speedups up to 1.68×." It outperforms Medusa-1 while using "88.7% fewer additional parameters (67M compared to 591M)."
- **Code:** Released at github.com/Equationliu/Kangaroo.

**Other details:** The subjects are Computation and Language (cs.CL) and Machine Learning (cs.LG). The DOI is 10.48550/arXiv.2404.18911.

**Title:** SpecExtend: A Drop-in Enhancement for Speculative Decoding of Long Sequences

**Authors:** Jungyoub Cha, Hyunjong Kim, Sungzoon Cho

**First version (v1) submitted:** Tue, 27 May 2025, 06:30:00 UTC

**Version history:**
- v1: Tue, 27 May 2025, 06:30:00 UTC (184 KB)
- v2: Fri, 22 Aug 2025, 08:45:04 UTC (189 KB)
- v3: Mon, 29 Sep 2025, 12:34:50 UTC (407 KB)
- v4: Mon, 19 Jan 2026, 09:43:38 UTC (227 KB), the current version

**Comments field (venue info):** The page has no comments field, so it gives no venue information.

**Journal-ref:** The page has no journal reference.

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract because of the quote-length limit. Here is a summary with short quotes:

- **Problem:** Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference, but it gets slower as inputs get longer. The authors note "significant drops even at moderate lengths," and say this early slowdown has received little study.
- **Approach:** SpecExtend is a "drop-in enhancement" that needs no retraining. It uses efficient attention methods, FlashAttention and Hybrid Tree Attention, to speed up the prefill and verification stages.
- **Main contribution:** The authors propose "Cross-model Retrieval," a KV cache eviction method. It uses the larger target model's attention scores to choose which context the smaller draft model keeps. This improves both the draft model's accuracy and its speed on long inputs.
- **Results:** Speedups reach "up to 2.84x on 16K-token long document summarization" and "up to 3.86x on long-form reasoning." Performance on short inputs stays on par with state-of-the-art frameworks.
- **Code:** Available at https://github.com/jycha98/SpecExtend

**Other details:** arXiv:2505.20776 [cs.CL], also listed under cs.AI and cs.LG. ACM classes I.2.7 and C.4. DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2505.20776. License: CC BY 4.0.

**Title:** SAM Decoding: Speculative Decoding via Suffix Automaton

**Authors:** Yuxuan Hu, Ke Wang, Xiaokang Zhang, Fanjin Zhang, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang

**First version (v1):** Sat, 16 Nov 2024, 02:02:49 UTC

**All versions:**
- v1: 16 Nov 2024, 02:02:49 UTC (690 KB)
- v2: 29 Nov 2024, 08:16:29 UTC (781 KB)
- v3: 16 Dec 2024, 10:48:28 UTC (1,281 KB)

**Comments field:** "16 pages, 9 figures, 9 tables". It gives no venue information.

**Journal-ref:** Not listed on the page.

**Abstract (summary):** I can't reproduce the full abstract verbatim because of the quote-length limit, so here is a paraphrase with short quotes:
- **Problem:** Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference without loss. Existing retrieval-based, model-free variants often use incomplete retrieval resources and inefficient retrieval, and they tend to work only in certain domains.
- **Method:** The authors propose a retrieval-based approach that uses a suffix automaton to draft tokens from both a common text corpus and the dynamically generated sequence.
- **Key claim:** Unlike n-gram matching, it "finds the exact longest suffix match." SAM updates and suffix retrieval take O(1) average time per generation step.
- **Integration:** It can work alongside existing methods, choosing a drafting strategy adaptively based on match length so it generalizes to more domains.
- **Results:** On Spec-Bench it is reported to be over 18% faster than other retrieval-based SD methods. Combined with EAGLE-2, it adds a 3.28%–11.13% speedup across LLM backbones of different sizes.
- **Code:** github.com/hyx1999/SAM-Decoding

For the exact wording, see arXiv:2411.10666.

I found the paper. Here's a summary:

**Paper basics**
- **Title:** Cassandra: Enabling Reasoning LLMs at Edge via Self-Speculative Decoding
- **arXiv ID:** 2605.26558, in the cs.AR (hardware architecture) category
- **Authors:** Soongyu Choi, Yuntae Kim, Muyoung Son and Joo-Young Kim (2026)
- **Submitted:** Tue, 26 May 2026

**The problem it tackles**
Reasoning LLMs spend a lot of time in the decode stage, where tokens are generated one at a time. Shortcuts that approximate the model also lower its accuracy, so speculative decoding, which keeps output quality the same, has become essential for efficient inference. The trouble is that existing methods still struggle to deliver strong low-batch performance without additional training, limiting practical deployment on consumer devices. The authors also say existing methods have high training cost, limited effectiveness in low-batch settings, additional memory overhead, and diminishing returns for long output sequences.

**How it works**
- Cassandra is an algorithm-hardware co-designed self-speculative decoding framework optimized for low-batch scenarios.
- It uses optimized pruning and mantissa truncation to pick out the most important values in the model weights and the KV cache. That trimmed-down version acts as a fast draft model that proposes candidate tokens, and the full-precision model then checks them in parallel.
- No extra training is needed, and the authors say it is significantly more efficient than earlier self-speculative methods that rely on layer skipping or structured KV compression.
- It also adds a lightweight encoder-decoder hardware module designed for seamless integration with commercial GPUs and NPUs, which cuts the cost of converting between Cassandra's data format and standard floating-point formats.

**Key results**
- Up to 2.41x speedup over the BF16 baseline without additional training.
- On Llama 3 8B running on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, Cassandra generates 1.81x more tokens under the same memory budget compared to Eagle-3, a state-of-the-art speculative decoding method.

**Funding:** The work was supported by an Institute for Information & communications Technology Promotion (IITP) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT).

**Outside commentary:** An automated review on Pith notes that the paper could meaningfully advance training-free speculative decoding for consumer hardware if the experimental results hold up. No human reviewer had weighed in there yet.

**Related papers** include CAS-Spec (cascade adaptive self-speculative decoding), SparseSpec (sparse self-speculative decoding for reasoning models), and SWIFT (on-the-fly self-speculative decoding by skipping layers).

You can read the full paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26558.

The DFlash paper is on arXiv as **arXiv:2602.06036**, and it was accepted to ICML 2026.

**Paper details**
- **Authors:** Jian Chen, Yesheng Liang, Zhijian Liu (Z Lab), ICML 2026
- **Versions:** v1 posted Thu, 5 Feb 2026; v2 posted Thu, 28 May 2026
- **Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06036

**The problem it tackles**
Speculative decoding uses a fast "draft" model to guess upcoming tokens, and the main model checks those guesses in parallel. Existing methods still rely on autoregressive drafting, which remains sequential and limits practical speedups. Diffusion LLMs offer a promising alternative by enabling parallel generation, but current diffusion models typically underperform compared with autoregressive models.

**How DFlash works**
- It generates draft tokens in a single forward pass and conditions the draft model on context features extracted from the target model. This makes drafting efficient, with high-quality outputs and higher acceptance rates.
- The key idea is that large autoregressive LLMs' hidden features implicitly contain information about multiple future tokens. In effect, the draft model becomes a diffusion adapter that uses the deep context features of the large target model.
- The draft model reuses the embedding and LM head from the target model. Only a few intermediate layers are trained, which keeps the parameter count small.
- In the comparison runs, DFlash uses block size 16 with a single denoising step.

**Results**
- Experiments show that DFlash achieves over 6x lossless acceleration across a range of models and tasks, with up to 2.5x higher speedup than the state-of-the-art method EAGLE-3.
- On Qwen3-4B/8B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct, the paper reports average acceptance lengths of 5.5–6.5 and end-to-end speedups of 2.2–6.1× over standard autoregressive decoding.
- Speedups hold up under sampling (temperature=1) and with thinking mode on, at roughly 4.5× for reasoning models.

**A caveat on the numbers**
A commenter on alphaXiv who tried to reproduce the results found that under the same conditions, EAGLE-3's token generation speed was more than twice DFlash's. They pointed to a possible timing mismatch: the EAGLE timing includes both the prefill and decoding stages, while the DFlash timing counts only decoding. This comes from a public comment, not a formal rebuttal.

**Code and follow-up work**
- The code is at github.com/z-lab/dflash. The project page says DFlash supports SGLang for production serving and Transformers for quick experimentation. The vLLM Speculators docs also cover DFlash.
- There are follow-ups as well: DFlash2, which adds local convolution and candidate selection, and DSpark, which builds on DFlash with a sequential Markov head and a confidence head.

SpecExtend was published in **Findings of ACL 2026**. I found no sign that it was accepted at EMNLP, AAAI or ICLR.

**Where it was published**
- The ACL Anthology lists it as: Jungyoub Cha, Hyunjong Kim, and Sungzoon Cho. 2026. SpecExtend: A Drop-in Enhancement for Speculative Decoding of Long Sequences. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026, pages 43366–43377, San Diego, California, United States.
- The preprint is on arXiv as [2505.20776](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20776).
- There are also two OpenReview pages for it (forum id 170GODIkgT and PDF id ooAUUimGLg). The results don't say which venue those submissions were for, so they can't confirm an ICLR or EMNLP acceptance.

**What the paper does**
- **The problem:** Speculative decoding is a widely used technique for accelerating inference in large language models (LLMs), but its performance degrades as input length grows, with significant drops even at moderate lengths. The authors trace this to two causes: (1) increased latency in the forward passes of both target and draft models due to the quadratic complexity of standard attention, and (2) reduced draft accuracy, as the draft model is typically smaller and trained only on short sequences.
- **The method:** SpecExtend integrates efficient attention mechanisms such as FlashAttention and Hybrid Tree Attention to accelerate prefill and verification steps. It also adds Cross-model Retrieval, a novel KV cache eviction strategy that leverages the target model's attention scores to dynamically select relevant context for the smaller draft model. None of this needs extra training.
- **Results:** It speeds up speculative decoding by up to 2.84× on 16K-token long summarization and up to 3.86× on long reasoning. It also improves the average accepted length by up to 2.55× on inputs of up to 16K tokens, outperforming static eviction strategies.
- **Setup:** The tests used both standard LLMs and EAGLE draft models. For summarization, the base models were Vicuna-7B-16K (Chiang et al., 2023) and LongChat-7B-16K (Li et al., 2023).
- **Code:** https://github.com/jycha98/SpecExtend

I found the paper, but none of the search results show it being published at NAACL. Every source lists it as an arXiv preprint.

**Paper details**
- **Title:** Inference with Reference: Lossless Acceleration of Large Language Models (arXiv:2304.04487, April 2023)
- **Authors:** Nan Yang, Tao Ge, Liang Wang, Binxing Jiao, Daxin Jiang, Linjun Yang, Rangan Majumder, Furu Wei
- **How others cite it:** A KDD 2024 paper (Lookahead) cites it as ArXiv, abs/2304.04487, 2023, not as a conference paper.

**What it does**
- The authors propose LLMA, an LLM accelerator to losslessly speed up Large Language Model (LLM) inference with references.
- The idea came from noticing that there are abundant identical text spans between the decoding result by an LLM and the reference that is available in many real world scenarios (e.g., retrieved documents).
- **How it works:** LLMA first selects a text span from the reference and copies its tokens to the decoder and then efficiently checks the tokens' appropriateness as the decoding result in parallel within one decoding step.
- **Main result:** It reaches over 2x speed-up for LLMs with identical generation results as greedy decoding in many practical generation scenarios where significant overlap between in-context reference and outputs exists (e.g., search engines and multi-turn conversations).
- **Advantage over earlier methods:** Speculative Decoding and Speculative Sampling need to introduce an additional efficient drafter. LLMA doesn't need a separate draft model.

**Experiments**
- **Models and data:** The paper was evaluated using the LLaMA model family (7B, 13B, and 30B parameters) across three primary scenarios using the MS-MARCO dataset. The three scenarios are retrieval-augmented generation, cache-assisted generation and multi-turn conversation.
- **Example speedup:** the 7B model's throughput increased from ~24 tokens/sec to nearly 60 tokens/sec in RAG settings.

If you need to know whether this work appeared at NAACL, possibly under a different title, I can look it up in the ACL Anthology.

I found the paper on the ACL Anthology. Here are the details:

**Citation**
- **Authors:** Yuxuan Hu, Ke Wang, Xiaokang Zhang, Fanjin Zhang, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, and Jing Zhang.
- **Venue:** Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 12187–12204, Vienna, Austria.
- **ACL Anthology page:** https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.595/ (PDF: https://aclanthology.org/2025.acl-long.595.pdf)
- **Citekey / DOI:** hu-etal-2025-sam, DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.595
- **arXiv preprint:** 2411.10666

**Summary of the abstract**
- The paper presents a new retrieval-based speculative decoding method. It adapts the suffix automaton (SAM) to generate drafts quickly and accurately, using both the text being generated and a static text corpus.
- Existing methods use n-gram matching. SAM-Decoding instead finds the exact longest suffix match, and each generation step of SAM update and suffix retrieval takes O(1) time on average. It can also be combined with existing methods, choosing a drafting strategy based on match length so it works across more domains.
- **Results:** On Spec-Bench, the method is 18% faster than other retrieval-based speculative decoding methods. Combined with EAGLE-2, it adds a further 3.28%–11.13% speedup across LLM backbones of different sizes.

**How it works**
The method uses two automata. The static SAM is built from a given text corpus. The dynamic SAM is built from the text being generated and grows as generation continues. The best of three candidate drafts is picked based on match length, and the LLM then verifies the draft to get the accepted tokens. The experiments were run on Vicuna-7B-v1.3, among other models, and evaluated on Spec-Bench, HumanEval, and HAGRID.

**Limitation:** One third-party review says the paper's limitation section admits that the static corpus isn't very diverse and may not match the output distribution of other LLMs.

The search found the OpenReview page for the paper: **ParallelSpec: Parallel Drafter for Efficient Speculative Decoding** (https://openreview.net/forum?id=SXvb8PS4Ud). It was posted around October 4, 2024. The search results don't show the review outcome or whether the paper was accepted, so check the forum page for the reviews and final decision.

**Authors and preprint:** The paper is also on arXiv as 2410.05589, by Zilin Xiao and 5 other authors.

**Problem:** Speculative decoding has proven to be an efficient solution to large language model (LLM) inference, where the small drafter predicts future tokens at a low cost, and the target model is leveraged to verify them in parallel. However, most existing works still draft tokens auto-regressively to maintain sequential dependency in language modeling, which the authors consider a big computational cost.

**Approach:**
- ParallelSpec learns to efficiently predict multiple future tokens in parallel using a single model, and it can be integrated into any speculative decoding framework that requires aligning the output distributions of the drafter and the target model with minimal training cost.
- It proposes to use a single lightweight model and several trainable [MASK] tokens to facilitate fast multi-token prediction as drafters, thereby mitigating the issue of drafting latency scaling linearly with the draft length.
- At each draft step, the drafter generates k tokens with a single forward pass, and then they are sent to the target model for parallel verification.
- The draft model shares the embedding layer and the language model head with the target model to minimize memory overhead, and they remain frozen to preserve the target model's output distribution.
- The authors also design a group-wise training strategy that allows efficient and accurate parallel drafter training.

**Experiments and results:**
- The authors choose two popular SD frameworks as testbeds, Medusa (Cai et al., 2024b) and EAGLE (Li et al., 2024b).
- Incorporating ParallelSpec into Vicuna-7B Medusa increases the average speedup ratio from 1.42× to 2.31×, leading to a 62.7% relative improvement.
- Adding it to EAGLE also achieves extra speedups across all target model settings, ranging from 2.55× to 2.84×.
- Overall, ParallelSpec accelerates baseline methods in latency up to 62% for Medusa and 9-17% for EAGLE on text generation benchmarks, and it achieves 2.84× overall speedup on the Llama-2-13B model using third-party evaluation criteria.
- Evaluation followed the SpecBench setup, and 68,000 ShareGPT conversations were used as training data.

I found the paper. Its NeurIPS 2024 title is a little different from the arXiv preprint: **"Kangaroo: Lossless Self-Speculative Decoding for Accelerating LLMs via Double Early Exiting."**

**Publication details**
- Full citation: Liu, Fangcheng; Tang, Yehui; Liu, Zhenhua; Ni, Yunsheng; Tang, Duyu; Han, Kai; Wang, Yunhe. Neural Information Processing Systems, 2024. DOI: 10.52202/079017-0381
- The paper was presented as a NeurIPS 2024 poster. On OpenReview it is listed as Published: 25 Sept 2024, Last Modified: 06 Nov 2024.
- It first appeared on arXiv as 2404.18911, under the shorter title "Kangaroo: Lossless Self-Speculative Decoding via Double Early Exiting." The first version was posted Mon, 29 Apr 2024.
- Links: the [proceedings abstract](https://proceedings.neurips.cc//paper_files/paper/2024/hash/16336d94a5ffca8de019087ab7fe403f-Abstract-Conference.html), the [PDF](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/16336d94a5ffca8de019087ab7fe403f-Paper-Conference.pdf), [OpenReview](https://openreview.net/forum?id=lT3oc04mDp), and the [code on GitHub](https://github.com/Equationliu/Kangaroo).

**What the paper does**
- **Problem:** Speculative decoding usually needs a separate draft model, and training separate draft model to achieve a satisfactory token acceptance rate can be costly and impractical.
- **First early exit:** Kangaroo leverages the shallow sub-network and the LM Head of the well-trained target LLM to construct a self-drafting model. To check the drafts, the self-verification stage only requires computing the remaining layers over the early-exited hidden states in parallel.
- **Adapter:** The authors train a small adapter on top of the sub-network to close the gap with the full model. It consists of only one multi-head attention and two normalization layers.
- **Second early exit:** They dynamically halt the small model's subsequent prediction during the drafting phase once the confidence level for the current step falls below a certain threshold. For tree decoding, the method dynamically adjusts the depth and width of the token tree based on the conditional probability distribution of the self-drafting model.
- **Results:** Kangaroo achieves walltime speedups up to 2.04×, outperforming Medusa-1 with 88.7% fewer additional parameters. The earlier arXiv version reported a smaller result: speedups up to 1.68× on Spec-Bench, with 67M additional parameters compared to Medusa-1's 591M.

The author lists differ slightly: the BibTeX on the GitHub page cites the arXiv preprint with six authors, while the NeurIPS proceedings version adds Duyu Tang.

LogitSpec was accepted to **Findings of ACL 2026**.

**Publication:** The ACL Anthology citation lists the authors as Tianyu Liu, Qitan Lv, Hao Li, Xing Gao, Xiao Sun, and Xiaoyan Sun. 2026. LogitSpec: Accelerating Retrieval-based Speculative Decoding via Next Next Token Speculation. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026, pages 33070–33092, San Diego, California, United States. The authors are from the University of Science and Technology of China and Shanghai AI Laboratory.

**History:** The arXiv preprint (2507.01449) has three versions: v1 on Wed, 2 Jul 2025, v2 on Mon, 12 Jan 2026, and v3 on Wed, 29 Apr 2026. There is also an OpenReview page for the paper from October 2025. The search results don't say which venue that page belongs to or how it was decided, so it was likely an earlier submission, but I can't confirm that.

**What it does:**
- **Problem:** Retrieval-based speculative decoding relies on a matching paradigm to retrieve the most relevant reference as the draft tokens, where these methods often fail to find matched and accurate draft tokens.
- **Key idea:** The logit of the last token can not only predict the next token, but also speculate the next next token. Drafting happens in two steps: (1) utilizing the last logit to speculate the next next token; (2) retrieving relevant reference for both the next token and the next next token.
- **Evidence for the idea:** One summary reports that over 50% of steps see the next next token in the top-60 entries for various models and tasks. For Llama 3.1 8B with a large 128K vocabulary, this percentage even increases to 64% within top-60 entries of the last logit.
- **Results:** The method is training-free and plug-and-play, which can be easily integrated into existing LLM inference frameworks. It can achieve up to 2.61× speedup and 3.28 mean accepted tokens per decoding step. It was compared against retrieval-based baselines (Lookahead, REST, PLD) and a vanilla draft-model-based SpS (using Vicuna-68M).
- **Code:** https://github.com/smart-lty/LogitSpec

**Title:** "LogitSpec: Accelerating Retrieval-based Speculative Decoding via Next Next Token Speculation"

**Authors:** Tianyu Liu, Qitan Lv, Hao Li, Xing Gao, Xiao Sun, and Xiaoyan Sun

**Venue:** *Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026* (San Diego, California, United States, July 2026), pages 33070–33092. Anthology ID: 2026.findings-acl.1655; DOI: 10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.1655.

**Abstract (summary):**
- **Background:** Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference. A small draft model proposes tokens, and the target model then checks them in parallel. Retrieval-based variants remove the draft model entirely, which cuts drafting overhead and makes deployment easier.
- **Problem:** These retrieval methods depend on matching, and they "often fail to find matched and accurate draft tokens."
- **Method:** The authors introduce LogitSpec, which widens the retrieval range. It rests on the observation that the final token's logit can predict the next token and "also speculate the next next token." Drafting happens in two stages:
  1. The last logit is used to guess the token two positions ahead.
  2. References are retrieved for both the next token and that following token.
- **Properties:** The method needs no training and is plug-and-play, so it fits easily into existing inference frameworks.
- **Results:** Across many text generation benchmarks, it reaches up to a 2.61× speedup and 3.28 mean accepted tokens per decoding step.

**Title:** SpecExtend: A Drop-in Enhancement for Speculative Decoding of Long Sequences

**Authors:** Jungyoub Cha, Hyunjong Kim, Sungzoon Cho

**Venue:** *Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026* (San Diego, California, July 2026), pages 43366–43377. Editors: Maria Liakata, Viviane P. Moreira, Jiajun Zhang, David Jurgens. Published by the ACL. DOI: 10.18653/v1/2026.findings-acl.2153

**Abstract (summarized):**
Speculative decoding speeds up LLM inference, but it becomes less effective as inputs get longer, "with significant drops even at moderate lengths." The authors say this early decline has received little study. They present SpecExtend, a plug-in improvement for long-sequence speculative decoding that needs no extra training.

- **Faster prefill and verification:** It uses efficient attention methods, namely FlashAttention and Hybrid Tree Attention.

**Authors:** Jian Chen, Yesheng Liang, Zhijian Liu

**Venue confirmation:** Yes, it is an ICML 2026 poster. It is scheduled for Thursday, July 9, 2026, 2:30–4:15 PM KST, in Hall A, poster #2006.

- **Problem:** Autoregressive LLMs decode one token at a time, which makes inference slow and leaves GPUs underused. **Title:** "Cassandra: Enabling Reasoning LLMs at Edge via Self-Speculative Decoding"

**Authors:** Soongyu Choi, Yuntae Kim, Muyoung Son, Joo-Young Kim

**First version (v1) submitted:** Tuesday, 26 May 2026, 05:12:44 UTC (5,865 KB)

**All versions:** Only v1 (26 May 2026) is listed.

**Comments field:** "To appear at ISCA 2026"

**Journal-ref:** None is listed on the page.

**Abstract (paraphrased):** I can't reproduce the full abstract word for word because of the quote-length limit, so here is a summary with short quotes.

- **Problem:** Speculative decoding speeds up LLMs without loss of accuracy. Reasoning models face heavy decode-stage costs, and approximation methods hurt accuracy. Current lossless techniques still "struggle to deliver strong low-batch performance without additional training," which makes them hard to use on consumer hardware.
- **Proposal:** Cassandra is "an algorithm-hardware co-designed self-speculative decoding framework optimized for low-batch scenarios."
  - It creates a draft model without training by selecting data at a fine-grained level.
  - It applies tuned pruning and mantissa truncation to keep the most important values in both the weights and the KV cache.
  - The draft proposes tokens quickly, and the full-precision model then checks them in parallel.
- **Comparison with prior work:** The authors say it is much more efficient than earlier self-speculative approaches that rely on layer skipping or structured KV compression.
- **Hardware:** A small encoder-decoder module cuts the cost of converting between Cassandra's formats and standard floating point. It is designed to fit into commercial GPUs and NPUs.
- **Results:**
  - It reaches "up to 2.41x speedup over the BF16 baseline without additional training."
  - On Llama 3 8B running on an RTX 4090, it produces 1.81x more tokens than Eagle-3 within the same memory budget.

**Subject:** Hardware Architecture (cs.AR)

**DOI:** https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.26558

content.content:
**Methods LongSpec builds on**

- **EAGLE**: The paper calls it the SoTA method and adopts its use of target-model hidden states and its autoregressive drafting idea. Cited limitations:
  - The draft model's "KV cache still grows linearly with context length"
  - Its training context length is 2048, "significantly shorter than the context lengths of modern LLMs"
  - It "cannot leverage Flash Attention," so it runs slower than Vanilla FA (Appendix E).
- **GliDe**: Inspires the cross-attention module that reuses the target model's KV cache. LongSpec also shares the embedding layer and LM head between draft and target models, which GliDe does not. GliDe's attention-mask approach to train–inference consistency is "incompatible with Flash Attention." The paper also notes that beam search in prior work "suffers from slow processing speed."
- **Medusa / EAGLE tree attention**: These apply prefix-tree masks but "only run on PyTorch's eager execution mode," so speed drops as sequences grow.

**Baselines compared**

- **MagicDec**: Described as "a simple prototype of TriForce." Its acceptance rates are competitive, but its speedup is lower because its draft model "becomes excessively heavy" at low batch sizes. It shows "negative acceleration around 0.7×" when γ≥3. On long reasoning tasks, its draft model "will completely degrade into the target model."
- **PLD**: A retrieval-based, n-gram method that "can even result in negative acceleration" when little retrieval is possible.
- **EAGLE and Token Recycling (TR)**: Compared in the appendix. TR "consistently underperforms LongSpec across the board."
- **Vanilla HF and Vanilla FA**: The plain target model with HuggingFace attention and with Flash Attention.

**Other long-context methods discussed in related work**

TriForce, MagicDec and QuantSpec "mainly utilize the target model with the sparse KV cache as the draft model." The paper argues these "computation-intensive draft models restrict the practical usage" across batch sizes, because full target models are "not sufficiently lightweight."

content.content:
**Built on:** AdaSpec extends vLLM. It adds "approximately 2000 lines of Python code" and uses vLLM's lookahead scheduler, which splits memory between the KV caches of the draft and target models. Its time model follows SmartSpec (Liu et al., 2024b), modeling forward-pass cost "as a linear function of the number of context tokens."

**Baselines compared in the evaluation:**
1. Autoregressive decoding.
2. Vanilla speculative decoding with fixed lengths of 1, 3, and 5.
3. A threshold-based dynamic method from the transformers library, described as "representing the state-of-the-practice method."
4. SpecInfer with tree width set to 1 ("SpecInfer\*"). The authors made this change because of "the inefficiency of tree-based inference strategies."

SmartSpec is not a direct baseline; it is only discussed as prior work. EAGLE and Medusa appear only as examples of static-length or self-draft methods. AdaServe is mentioned as contemporaneous work, but it targets tree-based decoding while AdaSpec targets sequential decoding.

**Draft model:** Yes, it is a separate small LM. The pairs are Vicuna-68M with Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-160M with Vicuna-33B, and Llama-3.2-1B with Llama-3.3-70B. The draft model runs at TP=1. The authors say the approach also applies to self-draft or MTP heads.

**Limitations of prior work cited:**
- **Static lengths:** most methods use a static speculative length found by "heuristic search on specific datasets and under fixed hardware configurations."
- **SmartSpec's granularity:** its "coarse-grained control still fails to adapt to the fine-grained variations."
- **Dynamic workloads:** fixed lengths "fail to adapt to dynamic changes in request patterns." At high load, long lengths waste verification compute; at low load, short lengths leave resources idle.
- **System configuration:** the methods are "Agnostic to system configurations." The best fixed length "loses its optimality" when the GPU or model pair changes.
- **SLOs:** "SLO violations" arise because variable token acceptance causes TPOT spikes, and existing work "overlook[s] token-level SLOs."
- **Batch uniformity:** a whole batch shares one length, "overlooking substantial differences in token acceptance probabilities."
- **Threshold method:** it keeps its length "near the preset maximum value of 8," and "relying solely on confidence scores cannot accurately determine optimal speculative lengths."

content.content:
**Prior verification methods it builds on or compares against**

- **Token-level speculative decoding** (Leviathan et al.; Chen et al.). This is the foundational single-token accept/reject scheme the paper sets out to improve.
- **SpecInfer's Recursive Rejection Sampling (RRS)**. It is cited as a valid tree verification algorithm.
- **RRS without replacement (RRSw)**. This refinement comes from Sequoia, EAGLE, Jeon et al., and Yang et al. RRSw is the actual experimental baseline: the authors "adopt the RRSw implementation in EAGLE" from the Spec-Bench repository, labeled "Tok.V".
- **Block Verification**. This is the main theoretical anchor. Traversal Verification matches its expected acceptance length on single chains and "inherits this optimality in the single-chain case."
- **Mentioned only in related work, not run as baselines:** SpecTr (optimal transport), Asps, SpecHub, and Greedy Sampling. Sequoia is also cited to argue that very large trees (768 nodes) could yield bigger gains.

**Drafting setup**

The paper does not use EAGLE-2 drafting. EAGLE-2 appears only in related work. The experiments instead use standalone draft/target pairs:

- Llama3.2-1B-Instruct drafting for Llama3.1-8B-Instruct
- Llama-68M drafting for Llama2-7B

Three tree shapes are tested: a chain, a binary tree, and the "EAGLE sparse tree" structure, all at depth 5. Evaluation is on Spec-Bench.

**Quoted limitations of prior work**

- Existing methods "inherit the token-level verification mechanism from vanilla speculative decoding to tree scenarios"
- Per-token acceptance "sacrifices global optimality for sequence-level acceptance"
- "Once a parent node is rejected, all its child nodes will be discarded"
- This results "in the wasting of drafted tokens"
- Overall, it leads "to suboptimal acceptance length"

**Reported gains over the RRSw baseline:** acceptance length improves by about 2.2% to 5.7%, with somewhat smaller throughput gains.

Abstract
We propose LLMA, an LLM accelerator to losslessly speed up Large Language
Model (LLM) inference with references. LLMA is motivated by the observation
that there are abundant identical text spans between the decoding result by an LLM
and the reference that is available in many real world scenarios (e.g., retrieved
documents). LLMA first selects a text span from the reference and copies its
tokens to the decoder and then efficiently checks the tokens’ appropriateness as the
decoding result in parallel within one decoding step. The improved computational
parallelism allows LLMA to achieve over 2× speed-up for LLMs with identical
generation results as greedy decoding in many practical generation scenarios where
significant overlap between in-context reference and outputs exists (e.g., search
engines and multi-turn conversations).

**Prior methods AMUSD builds on or compares against**

- **Foundation:** It builds on speculative decoding, which the paper attributes to Stern et al. (blockwise parallel decoding, NeurIPS 2018).
- **Related work cited only, not benchmarked:**
  - a speculative decoding survey (Xia et al.)
  - SpecInfer (tree-based verification)
  - Medusa (multiple decoding heads)
  - EAGLE
  - REST (retrieval-based)
  - DistillSpec
  - Draft & Verify (self-speculative)
  - Lookahead decoding
- The author calls these algorithmic advances "orthogonal to the systems-level parallelization we propose."
- **Experimental baselines:** Only two are tested: standard autoregressive decoding and conventional synchronous speculative decoding.

**PEARL or other parallel/asynchronous speculative decoding**
PEARL isn't mentioned. The paper cites no prior asynchronous or parallel draft/verify approach and presents its own method as "a novel asynchronous approach."

**Venue or workshop**
None is named. The page lists only arXiv:2410.17375v1 [cs.CL], dated 22 Oct 2024, under a CC BY 4.0 license.

**Draft/target model pair**
There is a single pairing: Llama-3.2-1B drafts and Llama-3.1-8B verifies. The autoregressive baseline uses Llama-3.1-8B alone. The models run at roughly 10 ms/token (draft) and 25 ms/token (verify) when standalone. Hardware was 4× A100 GPUs, with the draft and verify models on separate GPUs.

**Quoted limitations of standard speculative decoding**
- "it still faces limitations due to its synchronous nature"
- "alternates between distinct drafting and verifying phases"
- "allowing only one model to perform computations at any given time"
- "only one model (draft or verify) performs token generation at a time"
- "requiring draft and verify phases to strictly alternate"
- "the system must pause drafting to verify these tokens before proceeding"

**DFlash's Prior Work: What It Builds On, Compares Against, and Critiques**

**Directly compared in experiments**
- **EAGLE-3** is the main baseline, tested at tree sizes 16/60 on Qwen3 and 10/60 on LLaMA-3.1.
  - It relies on autoregressive drafting, which the authors call "not only inherently inefficient but also susceptible to error accumulation." They say this caps speedups "at approximately 2−3×."
  - To keep latency low, it is limited to "a single transformer layer."
  - It fuses target features only at the input, so with more depth "the information from target model becomes more and more diluted."
- **Native MTP** (multi-token prediction, appendix, Qwen3.5) is outperformed by DFlash, but no specific weakness is identified beyond lower speedup.
- **Vanilla autoregressive decoding** is the speedup reference point.

**Built upon**
- **Block diffusion** (Arriola et al.; Fast-dLLM v2; SDAR) provides the drafting paradigm, though DFlash changes the training recipe. Cited weaknesses:
  - Such models "typically underperform their autoregressive counterparts."
  - They often need "a high number of denoising steps."
- **Samragh et al.** supplies the core insight that LLM hidden states "implicitly contain information about multiple future tokens."
- **The EAGLE series** contributed the idea of using "feature-level context from the frozen target model."

**Discussed but not benchmarked**
These were excluded "due to lack of open-source implementation":
- **DiffuSpec / SpecDiff-2** use very large drafters (around 7B parameters), whose memory cost is "often prohibitively expensive." The resulting drafting latency limits speedups "to a modest 3−4×."
- **PARD** trains small models that "lack the modeling capacity of the target LLMs," giving "a speedup ceiling of approximately 3×." Naive small diffusion drafters like this lead "to poor acceptance length."
- **TiDAR** is noted as "not yet lossless."
- **Medusa** is described only as adding prediction heads with tree attention. No limitation is cited beyond the general point that most methods use sequential autoregressive drafting.

**Methods SpecExtend builds on**
- **FlashAttention / FlashDecoding:** FlashAttention speeds up the prefill stage for both models. FlashDecoding adds parallelism across the KV sequence length.
- **Hybrid Tree Attention:** This comes from LongSpec (Yang et al., 2025). It makes FlashDecoding work with tree-structured attention, and SpecExtend uses it to speed up target-model verification.
- **Drafting frameworks used as the base:** EAGLE, EAGLE-3, off-the-shelf small drafters (Vicuna-68M/LLaMA-68M), and SpecInfer/OPT-Tree tree drafting with dynamic expansion. Being drop-in lets SpecExtend "harness the powerful short-input performance" of these frameworks.

**Methods it compares against**
- TriForce, MagicDec, FlashDecoding and standard tree-based SD (Table 3).
- StreamingLLM, as a static cache-eviction baseline (Needle Retrieval test and ablation).
- LongSpec is left out of the comparison because it is training-based.

**Limitations the paper cites**
- **TriForce and MagicDec:** Both draft from the base model's sparse KV cache. That targets the KV-cache bottleneck, but slowdown "arises much earlier than this bottleneck shift." They "yield little speedup due to drafting with the slow base model that has large weights." In the moderate regime, "model weights remain the dominant memory bottleneck." MagicDec also fails "to yield meaningful speedup on short inputs."
- **StreamingLLM:** As a static policy, its accuracy drops "when tasks require finer-grained use of past context," because of "loss of global context" and greater target-draft divergence.
- **LongSpec:** It needs dedicated training, and "retraining draft models on long contexts is costly." The authors concede SpecExtend does not beat it.
- **EAGLE-3:** Its accuracy "drops sharply beyond 2K tokens, even falling below EAGLE-1."
- **Draft models in general:** They are smaller and typically "trained only on short sequences."

SuffixDecoding is compared directly against EAGLE-2/3, Token Recycling and PLD. **REST and Lookahead are never mentioned** in the provided text.

**Methods it builds on**
- **Suffix trees:** It uses suffix trees from Weiner (1973), with online construction following Ukkonen (1995).
- **Tree-based speculation:** This comes from SpecInfer, which "introduced tree-based speculation."
- **EAGLE-3 in the hybrid mode:** If the suffix score falls below a threshold τ, the method switches to "a fall-back speculation method, such as EAGLE-3."

**Methods it is compared against**
- EAGLE-2 and EAGLE-3 (plus EAGLE-1 in the appendix tables)
- Prompt Lookup Decoding (PLD)
- Token Recycling
- On the end-to-end vLLM test, only PLD, because no draft models exist for the OpenHands LLM.

**Limitations cited**
- **Model-based methods (EAGLE):**
  - They "can use significant GPU time when speculating long sequences."
  - They can incur "memory contention and kernel-level transitions."
  - On SWE-Bench, EAGLE-2/3 "fail due to their maximum sequence length limitations."
  - They also need trained draft models, and none existed for the OpenHands LLM.
- **PLD:** Model-free methods like it "typically lack adaptivity." They speculate "a fixed number of tokens irrespective of acceptance likelihood," which wastes compute verifying unlikely drafts.
- **Model-free methods in general (PLD, Token Recycling, LLMA, ANPD):** They "rely on small reference texts and lack adaptive speculation."
- **Token Recycling:** It also failed on long-context SWE-Bench tasks. Its speculation overhead there was much higher, about 10.6 ms per token versus roughly 0.18 ms for SuffixDecoding.
- **Conceded limitation of SuffixDecoding:** On open-ended Spec-Bench, SuffixDecoding alone loses to EAGLE-2/3 and Token Recycling. The hybrid variant recovers the lead.

**Is it lossless?**
Yes, the authors claim so. They state it "exactly preserves the output distribution of the LLM," and it matched the base model's 37.2% on SWE-Bench Verified. Verification follows standard speculative decoding, "accepting tokens up to the first discrepancy." One caveat: the ablations use a simulated verifier that is valid only "for greedy sampling."

# Cassandra's relationship to prior speculative decoding methods

**Note:** LayerSkip and TriForce do not appear anywhere in the provided text.

## Methods compared directly in experiments (Fig. 13, §VII-B)

The authors ran official open-source implementations of four methods against Cassandra-1:

- **Draft&Verify** (training-free, skips layers)
  - It skips 18 attention layers but only 9 FFN layers, so the draft "must still load 70.7% of the original model's parameters."
  - Its Bayesian search needs "approximately 1.5 hours of Bayesian optimization on A100."
- **MagicDec** (training-free, sparse KV retrieval)
  - Because it depends on KV cache pruning, it performs poorly at low batch sizes, "occasionally even performing slower than the baseline."
- **Lookahead Decoding** (training-free, n-gram based)
  - It trails Cassandra "particularly on LongBench and LiveCodeBench."
  - It still reached 1.40× on AIME2025 and 1.46× on GPQA-Diamond.
- **EAGLE-3** (training-based)
  - It needs "approximately two days of training on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs."
  - It keeps a separate draft model, which adds memory overhead. Cassandra generates "1.81× more tokens" within the same memory budget.
  - It beat Cassandra on AIME2025 and GPQA-Diamond. However, its gains are "heavily biased toward the characteristics of its training data" and weaken on long-sequence tasks.

## Methods mentioned only in related work

- **SWIFT** builds its draft by skipping layers, similar to Draft&Verify.
- **QuantSpec** simplifies the KV cache through reduced-precision quantization.
- The authors' general criticism of these self-speculative methods:
  - They depend on "coarse-grained approximations" and mainly target attention and the KV cache.
  - Their gains "remain limited in low-batch scenarios," where loading FFN weights is the real bottleneck.
  - Where they add separate draft weights, they incur "non-negligible memory capacity overhead."

## Other baselines

- **Classic two-model speculative decoding** (Leviathan; Chen) is the conceptual foundation. Its independent draft model is criticized for its memory overhead.
- **SmoothQuant W8A8 / INT8 via vLLM** serves as a quantization baseline, reaching only about 1.3× speedup.

## Is the output lossless?

It depends on the configuration.

- **The verification mechanism is exact.** Pruning and truncation affect only the draft. Verification uses full data, and rejection sampling ensures outputs are "probabilistically identical to those of the target model." The draft is "a strict subset of the original model parameters."
- **Cassandra-1 is lossless.** Its exponents are unary-coded, which preserves "full numerical accuracy." Its scores matched BFloat16 exactly.
- **Cassandra-2 is not strictly lossless.** Its MX-based exponent sharing is described as having "minor accuracy loss," and its accuracy was "comparable to that of Smoothquant." This is why Cassandra-1 was the configuration used against the other speculative methods, since those all use a BF16 target.

# TriForce: Prior Limitations and the Methods It Builds On

## Limitations of prior approaches for long sequences

**1. Trained small draft models don't scale to long contexts**
- Training drafts to match the target's context length "requires massive computation".
- It is unclear "whether these small models can achieve the same accuracy with a context length around 1M".

**2. Training-free drafts using eviction caches speculate poorly**
- Such drafts "can result in poor speculating performance".
- Divergence from the target keeps growing as sequences lengthen (Fig. 2a), so acceptance rates fall.
- Fig. 2 also notes that "temperature sensitivity signals a lack of robustness".

**3. StreamingLLM and H2O are lossy**
- "discarded KV pairs cannot be restored", which risks "hallucination and contextual incoherency".
- They "inevitably and irrecoverably discard KV pairs".
- On needle retrieval, their acceptance rates collapse to 0.0519 and 0.0739.
- They "might not be directly applicable" to tasks that need full long-context understanding.

**4. The KV cache becomes the bottleneck**
- KV cache "grows linearly with sequence length" and eventually dominates memory, beyond the cost of the model weights.

**5. Staged or cascade speculation targets the wrong bottleneck**
- These methods focus "on model weights at every stage", whereas TriForce targets weights and KV cache separately.

**6. Other methods fall short in specific ways**
- Medusa-style self-speculation requires "training efforts" (the paper treats it as orthogonal).
- Skipping Layers still uses 68% of the KV cache, compared with TriForce's 3%.
- REST relies on "an external predefined datastore".

## Prior work TriForce builds on

- **Standard speculative decoding (Leviathan et al.; Chen et al.):** TriForce's correctness guarantee is "identical to the standard speculative decoding algorithm".
- **Self-speculation (Draft & Verify, Zhang et al.):** drafted tokens are "self-verified" by the target model using the full cache.
- **StreamingLLM:** reused as the cache for the small draft model at the bottom level of the hierarchy.
- **SpecInfer (Miao et al.):** supplies the JackFram/Llama68M initial draft model.
- **Staged and cascade speculation (Spector & Re; Chen et al.):** hierarchical speculation "shares similarities with these approaches".
- **Attention-sparsity work (H2O, StreamingLLM, Deja Vu, Scissorhands):** motivates using a partial KV cache as the draft cache.
- **Sequoia and tree-based methods:** shown to be compatible with TriForce in ablations, not part of the core design.

Retrieval-based sparse KV drafting is TriForce's own contribution rather than a borrowed method. It chunks the cache, scores the average key of each chunk, and retrieves the top chunks, inspired by classic information retrieval (Singhal et al.).

- REST relies on "an external predefined datastore".

## Prior work TriForce builds on

- **Standard speculative decoding (Leviathan et al.; Chen et al.):** TriForce's correctness guarantee is "identical to the standard speculative decoding algorithm".
- **Self-speculation (Draft & Verify, Zhang et al.):** drafted tokens are "self-verified" by the target model using the full cache.
- **StreamingLLM:** reused as the cache for the small draft model at the bottom level of the hierarchy.
- **SpecInfer (Miao et al.):** supplies the JackFram/Llama68M initial draft model.
- **Staged and cascade speculation (Spector & Re; Chen et al.):** hierarchical speculation "shares similarities with these approaches".
- **Attention-sparsity work (H2O, StreamingLLM, Deja Vu, Scissorhands):** motivates using a partial KV cache as the draft cache.
- **Sequoia and tree-based methods:** shown to be compatible with TriForce in ablations, not part of the core design.

Retrieval-based sparse KV drafting is TriForce's own contribution rather than a borrowed method. It chunks the cache, scores the average key of each chunk, and retrieves the top chunks, inspired by classic information retrieval (Singhal et al.).

**Baselines compared (Section 4.1, Tables 1–3)**

PEARL uses four training-free baselines plus auto-regressive decoding:
- **Vanilla speculative decoding (SpS):** Leviathan et al. 2023 and Chen et al. 2023. For fairness, each pair uses its tuned optimal γ (Appendix D.2).
- **Ouroboros:** Zhao et al. 2024.
- **Lookahead Decoding:** Fu et al. 2024.
- **Assisted Generation:** Joao Gante, 2023, which picks the next draft count heuristically.

EAGLE is **not** a baseline. It appears only in Related Work, along with Medusa, Self-speculative decoding, Glide, DistillSpec and SpecInfer. The authors say these methods "do not address the parallelism issue" and that PEARL is orthogonal to them.

**Other parallel/asynchronous SD methods**

The paper does not mention SpecBranch, AMUSD or any other parallel or asynchronous SD work. Its related work treats parallelism as a gap that PEARL alone fills.

**Draft/target pairs**
- CodeLlama 7B & 34B, and 7B & 70B
- Llama 2 7B & 70B
- Llama 3.1 8B & 70B (no Ouroboros or Lookahead results, because of transformers version constraints)
- DeepSeek-Coder 1.3B & 33B, and 6.7B & 33B

**Phrases on mutual waiting**
- "the target model gets stuck when the draft model is guessing tokens, and vice versa"
- "directly incurred by the asynchronous execution of the draft model and the target model"
- "exacerbated due to the fixed draft length in speculative decoding"
- "the mutual waiting problem exists at any timestamp"
- For CodeLlama 7B/34B: "generating 6 draft tokens is even 2 times than the time consumption for one verification step"

# SAM-Decoding: baselines, cited limitations, and combined methods

## Retrieval-based methods it compares against

The baselines are **Lookahead Decoding, PIA, PLD, and REST**. All four appear in Table 1 and are described in Related Work as methods that draft "through retrieval, utilizing n-gram matching."

- **General limitations (abstract):** existing methods "rely on incomplete retrieval resources, inefficient retrieval methods, and are constrained to certain domains."
- **Single retrieval source:** "PLD focuses on current text while REST uses a text corpus."
- **PLD:** It "has poor theoretical computational complexity and limited applicability to larger text corpus." Its brute-force n-gram search is O(n²L).
- **REST:** It "uses suffixed arrays, which provides better complexity than PLD, but still not optimal complexity." Its cost is given as O(n² log L).
- **Domain restriction:** these methods "are unable to bring a noticeable acceleration in other domains."
- **Lookahead and PIA:** the paper gives no limitation specific to either one. They are only grouped with the other n-gram matching methods and outperformed in the experiments.

## Token Recycling

The paper does not treat Token Recycling as a retrieval method. It calls it "a model-free method different from the retrieval-based method," because it "utilizes the previously generated token distribution to generate drafts." It serves as a baseline and also as one of the auxiliary methods, in the SAM-Decoding[T] variant.

## LLMA

LLMA does not appear anywhere in the text.

## Model-based methods

- **EAGLE-2** is the only model-based method actually combined with SAM-Decoding, in the SAM-Decoding[E2] variant.
- **Medusa** is cited only as an example of model-based drafting and is never combined or benchmarked.
- **Shared limitation of model-based methods:** "they often fail to generate long draft tokens due to drafting overhead or decaying prediction accuracy."
- **HumanEval caveat:** adding SAM-Decoding barely changed EAGLE-2's throughput, because "the code generation task is less likely to copy the generated text."

content.content:
**Draft-model limitations REST cites**

- **Hard to build a good draft model.** It "must balance small size and strong predictive power while matching the vocabulary of the base model" and should "integrate well into a distributed system for serving."
- **Custom training is often needed.** Teams frequently have to "train a draft model specifically for their model and use cases." Section 3.2 says this means "carefully selecting or even training custom draft models for each new LLM."
- **Runtime cost.** Small-model drafters "require additional GPU memory and introduce complexity during inference."
- **Medusa and blockwise decoding** "train specialized modules to create a draft model." REST instead "eliminates the need for any additional training steps."

**Baselines compared**

- **Standard autoregressive decoding**, with both greedy and nucleus sampling.
- **Classic speculative decoding**, using a reproduced implementation sped up with torch.compile.
  - Draft LMs tested: Llama 68M, Llama 160M, TinyLlama 1.1B and TinyLlama-Chat 1.1B.
  - Draft lengths ranged from 1 to 15 tokens, and only the best configuration was reported.
- **Medusa is not an experimental baseline.** It only informs the choice of 64 draft tokens.
- **Ablation only:** random selection of retrieved candidates versus Trie-based selection.

**Results caveat**

The authors state "we do not claim that REST can outperform speculative decoding under all circumstances." On CodeLlama 13B greedy, speculative decoding is slightly faster (19.39 vs. 19.53 ms/token). The text also says the HumanEval speedup is "2.16× to 2.36×," but Table 1's lowest figure is 2.12×.

**Lossless under greedy and sampling?**

The paper claims yes for both. It does not use modified rejection sampling. Instead, it accepts drafts only "if they match the tokens sampled from the LLM." Tokens up to the first mismatch are kept and the rest are discarded. As a result, "the sequences produced using REST are identical to those generated by standard autoregressive generation."

Under nucleus sampling, sampling is less efficient but still lossless. The authors attribute the lower speedup to "the randomness introduced by nucleus sampling."

# Limitations of Prior Self-Speculative Methods Cited by Kangaroo

**General issue (intro)**
- Training a separate draft model is expensive: "the training of such task-specific models can be costly."
- Optimizing only acceptance while ignoring drafting latency "can lead to suboptimal end-to-end acceleration."

**Medusa**
- It uses "multiple time-independent FFN heads on top of the last decoder layer."
- It drafts quickly, but "its token acceptance rate is not yet satisfactory."

**Lookahead**
- Its acceptance on math reasoning is close to Kangaroo's.
- However, it suffers from "lower efficiency in generating draft tokens compared to Medusa."
- As a result, its end-to-end speedup falls slightly below Medusa's.

**REST (and LLMA)**
- The intro only describes how they draft: retrieving tokens from a database or copying spans from a reference.
- It then says broadly that "these approaches still present some challenges." No REST-specific weakness is named.

**Draft & Verify (layer skipping)**
- This critique comes from Related Work rather than the intro.
- It can reach high acceptance, but "the inference latency of the 'small model' is exceptionally high."

# Baselines Compared on Spec-Bench

The comparison covers Lookahead, Medusa and REST against Kangaroo, on Vicuna-7B and 13B using V100 GPUs. Draft & Verify was not benchmarked.

| Method | 7B avg speedup | 13B avg speedup |
|---|---|---|
| Lookahead | 1.29× | 1.04× |
| Medusa | 1.41× | 1.34× |
| REST | 1.43× | 1.23× |
| Kangaroo | 1.50× | 1.44× |

The adapter ablation also compares Kangaroo with Medusa directly. Kangaroo uses 67M added parameters versus Medusa's 591M, and achieves 1.50× versus 1.41× speedup.

**Frameworks it plugs into**

ParallelSpec replaces the drafter inside existing frameworks. The authors test it on "the popular speculative decoding framework Medusa" and on "state-of-the-art solution EAGLE." They describe it as able to "replace any drafter in existing SD frameworks" that align a drafter with its target model.

**Limitations cited**

- **Autoregressive drafters (e.g., EAGLE):** They "still generate token by token, resulting in a low arithmetic intensity." Drafting latency "still grows linearly with respect to the draft length."
- **Medusa-style designs:** These "rely on separate language model heads to decode future tokens." With vocabularies of 128K+ tokens, this design "would struggle even more with memory and computation."
- **Draft-length fixes (learned policies, confidence heuristics, tree optimization):** These "do not tackle the underlying issue" of linear scaling. They only reduce wasted compute.

**BiTA, PaSS, and mask-token decoding**

- **Mask-token parallel decoding:** This is the core idea. Parallel decoding is traced to machine translation (Mask-Predict, Ghazvininejad et al.), but its use in speculative decoding "remains under-explored." ParallelSpec appends k trainable "[MASK] tokens as prompt tokens" so one forward pass yields several future tokens.
- **PaSS (Monea et al., 2023):** It is credited with having "pioneered the use of parallel decoding in SD." It is criticized as "limited to a self-speculative framework," with "different generation sampling." Even so, the paper's modified sampling algorithm (§4.2) is built "following Monea et al. (2023)."
- **BiTA:** It is described as tuning "a small number of prompt parameters on a frozen target LM." BiTA and related methods are faulted because they either "fail to effectively learn the draft distribution" or "cannot achieve lossless acceleration."

ParallelSpec's alternative is a single lightweight trainable drafter that shares parameters across positions.
